Data handlers

Who they are: The individual (natural person) to whom the personal data relates. This is the person whose information is being collected, processed, or stored. entry.summary: I implemented Raft from the paper in Go — leader election, log replication, snapshotting, joint-consensus membership changes — with a linearizable key/value store on top. The difficult part wasn't implementing the happy path. It was finding the defects that only became reachable once log compaction removed the redundancy that had been hiding them. Adding snapshotting exposed three real bugs. A deterministic simulator I had built beforehand caught the subtlest one and pinned it to a single seed — seed 188 — which then reproduced it exactly throughout the diagnosis. The other two were caught by a storage conformance suite and a restart test. This post walks through each one, from trigger to regression test, along with the false positive I refused to count. entry.title: Late‑night push and the illusion of good enough
entry.summary: At 2:17 am, the terminal screamed “permission denied” as I tried to push the live‑publish branch to the staging server. I stared at the error, then at the diff that added a tiny wrapper around the model’s output to run a basic quality check before sending it to the web. The commit was meant to be a safety net, a single line that would block obviously malformed responses. In practice it felt like a Band‑Aid on a wound that keeps bleeding. I spent the next hour replaying the same request through the new gate, watching the check reject a perfectly valid answer because a stray newline tripped the length filter. That made me realize I had been too eager to call the feature “ready”. My opinion is simple: a quality check is only useful if you understand the failure modes, not if you assume the check itself is flawless. The bug forced me to step back and redesign the validation logic, separating syntactic sanity from semantic relevance. I also learned that “basic” in a commit message can be a dangerous understatement; it encouraged me to skip a proper test suite for the new path. Now the live‑publish endpoint refuses to serve anything that doesn’t pass the new filter, and I finally have a reproducible failure to write a test for. The night ended with a quiet terminal and a reminder that shortcuts rarely survive real traffic.

entry.title: Nix and Lix patch daemon flaws that allow local root
entry.summary:
The Nix and Lix projects jointly disclosed security flaws on October 13, 2026 that can be chained into root access on machines running their package-building daemons. Fixed releases came out the same day. Any multi-user Nix or Lix setup where untrusted users can reach the daemon should upgrade now. Nix is a package manager and build system that underpins the NixOS Linux distribution. Lix is a separate implementation of Nix. Both run a background service, the daemon, that builds software on behalf of local users. The joint advisory on NixOS Discourse lists several issues. The most serious lets a local user corrupt files that later run as root.

entry.title: Building a VAMP Ratio Monitor: Merchant and Portfolio Math in Practice
entry.summary:
The Visa Acquirer Monitoring Program (VAMP) ratio fits on a napkin: fraud reports plus disputes, divided by transactions. It is easy to get the formula right and the number wrong. A monitor that is off by a few basis points can show an acquirer as safe when it is not. This article walks through how to compute the ratio correctly. entry.title: Apache Kafka
entry.summary:
Apache Kafka is a powerful open-source distributed event streaming platform designed to handle real-time data feeds. It was originally developed by LinkedIn and is now maintained by the Apache Software Foundation. Kafka is widely used for building real-time data pipelines and streaming applications. Core Concepts of Apache Kafka
Topics: A Kafka topic is a category or feed name to which records are sent by producers. Topics are partitioned, meaning each topic can have multiple partitions to allow parallel processing. Example: A topic named user_activity could store logs of user actions on a website. Partitions: Each topic is divided into partitions, which are ordered, immutable sequences of records.
